Timeline::add_seconds¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signature¶

Timeline Timeline::add_seconds(int seconds) const

Add Integral Elapsed Seconds¶

add_seconds() adds a single signed count of exact one-billion-nanosecond intervals to every defined instant. It is the direct method for integral-second delays, clock corrections, and threshold windows when constructing a separate Duration would add no information.

This is epoch-axis arithmetic. It does not replace the displayed second field, round to a boundary, or preserve local wall-clock fields across timezone offset changes. Existing fractional nanoseconds remain attached to the shifted instant.

Example 1. Forty-five seconds crosses midnight without losing precision.

const auto source = pluss::timeline::make(
    "2024-12-31T23:59:30.123456789Z");
std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::timeline::format(
    source.add_seconds(45), "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"2025-01-01T00:00:15.123456789+00:00"

Positive, Negative, And Zero Counts¶

Positive counts move toward later instants, negative counts subtract elapsed seconds, and zero preserves the stored ticks. The returned timeline owns its result; the receiver remains unchanged.

Example 2. A negative count crosses into the previous minute.

std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::timeline::format(
    source.add_seconds(-90), "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"2024-12-31T23:58:00.123456789+00:00"

Example 3. Printing both a zero-shift result and the source makes the no-op and non-mutation contracts explicit.

const auto shifted = source.add_seconds(45);
std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::timeline::format(
    source.add_seconds(0), "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::timeline::format(
    source, "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"2024-12-31T23:59:30.123456789+00:00"
Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"2024-12-31T23:59:30.123456789+00:00"

Rank, Timezone, And Absence¶

The one integer argument applies elementwise to scalar and array timelines. No broadcasting is involved. The output retains shape and timezone metadata, follows logical strides, and propagates NaT. A zero-sized input returns the same zero-sized shape.

Example 4. Defined and absent values remain distinguishable after the shift.

const auto values = pluss::timeline::from_epoch(
    {1'704'067'200'123'456'789LL, pluss::Timeline::kNaT}, "UTC");
std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::timeline::format(
    values.add_seconds(1), "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["2024-01-01T00:00:01.123456789+00:00", "NaT"]

Overflow Is An Error¶

The int second count itself always scales safely into signed 64-bit nanoseconds, but the final addition can still exceed the epoch storage range for an instant near an endpoint. That addition is checked for every defined element. Overflow throws instead of wrapping.

Example 5. A near-maximum epoch tick cannot accept another second.

try {
  (void)pluss::timeline::from_epoch(
      std::int64_t{9'223'372'036'854'775'000LL}).add_seconds(1);
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "rejected\n";
}

Output¶

rejected
